title: The iconostasis
hookLine: a wall of icons between the nave and the altar

cards: From the back of a Byzantine church, you can barely see the altar. What you see is a wall: a screen of wood or stone running the width of the church, covered in painted faces on gold. Saints.
Angels. A mother and child. A man with a long beard holding a scroll.
Their eyes look straight out. In the middle there are doors, and during the liturgy they open, a deacon comes through with incense, and for a moment you glimpse the altar behind.
Then the doors close, and the faces are watching again.

teach.h: BETWEEN THE NAVE AND THE ALTAR.
teach.b: You met John of Damascus and the icons earlier on this path. First, what it is. The iconostasis stands between the nave, where the people pray, and the sanctuary, where the altar is.
It has a central pair of doors, the Royal or Holy Doors, and usually a smaller door on each side, for the deacons. Second, the order of it.

teach.h: CHRIST ON THE RIGHT, HIS MOTHER ON THE LEFT.
teach.b: To the right of the central doors, as you face it, is Christ; to the left, his mother, holding him.

Next to them often stand John the Baptist and the saint the church is named for, and in larger churches, rows above them: the great feasts, the apostles, the prophets. The whole story of salvation on one screen.
Third, why paint God at all.

teach.h: THE IMAGE OF THE INVISIBLE GOD.
teach.b: Paul writes of Christ, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who is the image of the invisible God." The Greek word for image there is eikon, icon.
Because God became flesh and could be seen, Catholics and Orthodox alike hold that he can be painted. The Second Council of Nicaea taught that the honor given to an image passes to the one it shows.
Nobody here is praying to wood.
Fourth, a window, not a wall. It looks like a barrier.

teach.h: SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.
teach.b: But its faces are the ones Hebrews calls "so great a cloud of witnesses." They're not keeping you out; they're showing you who's already inside, and when the doors open, the Church can see straight through to the altar.
The room is full before anyone gets there.

how: In Byzantine churches, Catholic and Orthodox, the iconostasis separates the nave from the sanctuary; people venerate its icons with a bow, the sign of the cross, a kiss or a candle, and the doors open at set moments of the liturgy.

games.q: the icon screen — tap the pairs.

s: the iconostasis is there to hide the altar from the people
its faces are a cloud of witnesses, and its doors open onto the altar during the liturgy.
Paul calls Christ the image of the invisible God
"who is the image of the invisible God." the Greek word is eikon.
Christians in the East pray to the wood and paint
the Second Council of Nicaea taught that honor given to an image passes to the one it shows.

games.q: you're arranging the icons on the screen, beside the central doors. where does the icon of Christ go?
o: to the right of the doors, as you face them.
games.why: Christ stands to the right of the Royal Doors, and his mother, holding him, to the left.

practice: Bring up a photograph of an iconostasis, or any icon you have, and pick one face to stay with, noticing how the eyes look straight out; let yourself be looked at for a minute.
If you pray, use an old prayer of the East on the breath, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me; if not, simply stay with the face.

wordCard.voice: Iconostasis. The screen of icons between the nave and the altar, with doors in the middle: a cloud of witnesses, and a window onto the altar. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the stand or screen of icons; eikon is the word for image.

carryVoice: Your line: the icon screen. A window onto the altar, crowded with witnesses. One thousand three hundred sixty days now.
